function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the task.  
I’ll also give you the exact file contents that you’ll need to add to the repo.

> **⚠️ Important** – I can’t actually clone or push to the remote repository from here, so you’ll have to run the commands locally on your machine.  
> If you run into any permission or SSH‑key issues, make sure you have the correct key added to your agent (`ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_rsa`) and that you’re logged into GitHub with the right permissions.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you already have the repo cloned, just `cd` into it.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo contains a simple Express app (`app.js`).  
A minimal Dockerfile for that looks like:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> Save this as `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can create a `k8s/` folder if it doesn’t exist):

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry/tag if needed
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> Adjust `image:` to point at the image you’ll push to your registry (e.g. `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`).

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      # Add your deployment step here if you want to auto‑deploy
      run: echo "Deploy step placeholder"
```

> *Tip:* If you want the workflow to automatically deploy to a cluster, add a step that runs `kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml` after logging into your cluster (you’ll need a kubeconfig secret).

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

If you want to keep the `k8s/` folder tidy, you can also add a `.gitkeep` file inside it:

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
touch k8s/.gitkeep
git add k8s/.gitkeep
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically on the `main` branch and build/push the Docker image to GitHub Container Registry.

---

## Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t nodejs-welcome:local .

# Verify Kubernetes manifests apply locally (requires a kubeconfig)
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

If everything looks good, you’re done! 🎉

---

### What if you hit an error?

| Error | Fix |
|-------|-----|
| `fatal: Could not read from remote repository.` | Make sure your SSH key is added to the agent and that you have write access to the repo. |
| `docker: Cannot connect to the Docker daemon` | Ensure Docker Desktop (or Docker Engine) is running. |
| `kubectl: command not found` | Install `kubectl` and configure it to point at your cluster. |

Feel free to reach out if you need help with any of those steps. Happy coding!
